description: The QUIC control plane's shared vectors (plan docs/plans/2026-11-14-quic-data-plane.md). Swift (`mac/Tests/QuicControlVectorTests.swift`, `QuicCapsVectorTests.swift`) and Kotlin (`QuicControlVectorTest.kt`, `QuicCapsVectorTest.kt`) run the same cases against their own code; the Rust core checks the ALPN constant (`mobile/native-src/quic-core/tests/vectors.rs`). Sections: `constants`, `actions` (the q.* actions inside a `cmd`), `channels` (the stream type header), `stat` (the `caps` field), `handshake` (who may send what, when), `gate` (who may open a session, what the controls show).

constants.description: Values both sides must share byte for byte. `alpn` is the TLS ALPN protocol id of the data plane (a version change bumps the suffix); `max_action_bytes` is the largest action string (UTF-8 bytes) either side parses; `accept_timeout_ms` is how long the side that asked waits for the other side's accept (and how long the phone waits for its user).

actions.description: The q.* actions that open and close a QUIC session, as the JSON string inside a `cmd`. `kind: parse` — `text` (a `{PAD}` marker is replaced by `pad`: `{char, to_bytes}` makes the whole text exactly that many UTF-8 bytes, `{char, count}` repeats the character) parsed with `allow_echo` (default false); `expect.result` is `action` (and `encoded`, the canonical form of the parsed action: keys in alphabetical order, no whitespace, session id lower case), `unknown` (a JSON object whose `a` is missing or not one of the five: ignored quietly) or `invalid` with a short `code`. `kind: encode` — an action object and the exact canonical string it must encode to; every encoded string must also parse back to itself.

channels.description: The first varint of every data stream names its channel: 1 file (bidi), 2 screen (uni), 3 camera (uni). `kind: header` — the bytes (`hex`) a sender writes for a channel (the shortest varint) and its stream `direction`. `kind: parse` — the first varint of `hex` read by a receiver: `channel` + `consumed` bytes, `unknown` (any other value, with the `value`), or `needMoreBytes`. Every QUIC varint length (1, 2, 4, 8 bytes) is read; a longer-than-necessary encoding is accepted (RFC 9000 allows it); only the first varint is consumed.

stat.description: `caps` is an array of capability names. Absent (or not an array) means 'no information': the receiver keeps what it has, so a battery or proximity stat never clobbers it. An array SETS the known capabilities (unknown names and non-string items are ignored; an empty array means 'supports none'). Today the only known name is `q1`; names are exact (case-sensitive). When the peer goes offline the set is cleared; until a stat with `caps` arrives, the peer is treated as not supporting QUIC. `kind: parse` — a decoded stat object and the update `QuicCaps.parse` must give (`absent` or `set` with `caps`). `kind: sequence` — steps applied in order to a fresh PeerCaps (`stat` with a stat object, `offline`), and the set expected after each step. `kind: available` — `quicAvailable` is true only on the LAN-direct link AND with `q1` known. `kind: advertise` — what a side writes into its own stat: [`q1`] when it supports QUIC, nothing otherwise.

handshake.description: The handshake rules of one session (`side` mac|phone, `asker` = this side sent the q.req, `start_ms`, optional `timeout_ms` for the accept wait, default 60000). `initial` is the phase at the start; each step is `send` (this side wants to send `action`), `receive` (the peer's `action` arrives) or `tick` (the clock reaches `at_ms`), with `expect` = `{applied: phase}` or `{ignored: code}` (for send/receive) or `{phase}` (tick), and an optional `then` = the phase the session must be in afterwards. A phase is `{name, deadline_ms?}` (awaitingAccept, awaitingUser, awaitingOffer, mayOffer, offered) or `{name: closed, close: ended|timedOut|rejected, reason?}`. The offer is always the Mac's; with the phone as the asker there is no accept step; an offer before the accept is ignored; after `closed` everything is ignored.

gate.description: Who may open a QUIC session, and what the controls show. `incoming`: a peer's q.req arrives; the answer is `busy` (a session is already active; checked FIRST so a running session is never disturbed), `relay` (the link is not the LAN-direct one), `unsupported` (this side does not serve that kind) or `proceed`. `visible`: whether QUIC controls are shown at all: only on the LAN-direct link AND when the peer announced `q1` (the same rule as `stat.available`). `outgoing`: this side wants to ask: `hidden` (the peer never announced `q1`: nothing to ask), then the same order busy, relay, unsupported, proceed. Both the Mac (`QuicGate`, Swift) and the phone (`QuicGate`, Kotlin) run every case.
